surveyDefinition.title: Online Grocery Delivery — consumer survey (North America)
surveyDefinition.studyPurpose: Identify which of 4 behavioural segments each consumer respondent belongs to, based on their online grocery delivery usage patterns, price sensitivity, and service expectations.

segments.name: Convenience-Driven Customers
segments.description: Order online at least weekly, often subscribe to a membership for free delivery, and are willing to pay for the convenience. They are less price-sensitive and prioritize time savings and reliability.

segments.name: Value-Optimizing Shoppers
segments.description: Order regularly but actively compare prices, use promotions, and may switch between services to get the best deal. They are sensitive to fees and markups and will adjust their behaviour to minimize cost.

segments.name: Occasional Emergency Users
segments.description: Order infrequently, only when too busy or in a pinch. They are price-sensitive and do not subscribe, often paying per order and complaining about fees.

segments.name: Quality-Focused Households
segments.description: Order regularly, often for weekly meal planning, and are willing to pay for quality and reliability. They are less price-sensitive but very concerned about substitutions, cold chain, and accurate orders.

surveyDefinition.whatThisSurveyIs: A segmentation study of Online Grocery Delivery buyers in North America. It asks how people use Online Grocery Delivery, how they choose it, and what would make them switch — then sorts respondents into the behavioural groups defined below. Questions stay at category level: no named brands, and nothing about adjacent categories.
surveyDefinition.whoseContextThisIs: Adults in North America who buy or use Online Grocery Delivery for personal or household use. Respondents qualify if they: Primary or shared decision-maker for household grocery purchases; Has used an online grocery delivery service in the past 3 months; Pays for the service personally (not reimbursed by an employer). Excluded: Businesses or institutions purchasing for resale or commercial use; Individuals who only use click-and-collect (curbside pickup) without delivery; People who have never ordered groceries online.
surveyDefinition.whyTheseRespondents: Household consumers buy groceries online, pay for them (either per order or via subscription), and decide what to order. Businesses also purchase through the same platforms for office or commercial use, making it a dual-motion market. The consumer side is the primary and dominant buyer.
respondentBehaviours: Orders groceries online at least once a month
Values convenience and time savings over in-store shopping
Uses mobile apps or websites for ordering
May subscribe to delivery membership programs (e.g., Instacart+, Amazon Fresh)
Often plans weekly or bi-weekly grocery hauls
whatIsDeliberatelyNotAsked: Age or household income as behavioural questions — no finding in this survey is driven by them. They are asked once, at the end, in Profiling, and used only to cross-tabulate the behavioural results.
Brand, company or manufacturer names — the survey stays at category level so findings are not tied to one competitor set.
Where the respondent lives — region is chosen when viewing the results, so asking it again would waste a question.
surveyDefinition.howToReadTheNumbers: Percentages are simulated from a persona-weighted panel of 2,500 synthetic respondents built from real market evidence, not from fieldwork. Single-choice, ranking and rating-scale questions sum to 100%. Multi-select questions do not — each option is an independent share of respondents choosing it. The N shown on each question is the display base for that item.

sections.label: Usage Context & Ordering Behaviour
sections.covers: Establish how respondents use online grocery delivery, including frequency, household role, and the occasions that drive ordering.

sections.label: Purchase Journey & Channel Choice
sections.covers: Understand what triggers an order, how respondents choose between services, and their typical spend and subscription behaviour.

sections.label: Service Requirements & Trade-offs
sections.covers: Identify the must-have service features, quality cues, and the trade-offs respondents are willing to make on price, fees, and delivery windows.

sections.label: Satisfaction, Loyalty & Churn Risk
sections.covers: Measure overall satisfaction, pain points, switching triggers, and future usage intent.

structure.storyline: Questions run in a planned narrative order: broad and easy first, specific and sensitive last.
structure.storylineSummary: This survey covers the consumer motion of online grocery delivery in North America. It starts by establishing who the respondent is in terms of their ordering behaviour and household role, then moves through their purchase journey, including triggers, service choice, and spend. It then explores their service requirements and trade-offs, and finally measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent. The story is designed to separate the four segments based on their frequency, price sensitivity, and quality focus.

targetCustomer.summary: Adult consumers of Online Grocery Delivery in North America — who Primary or shared decision-maker for household grocery purchases; Has used an online grocery delivery service in the past 3 months; Pays for the service personally (not reimbursed by an employer). The consumer audience is the primary buyer and user of online grocery delivery. They make the purchase decision and pay for the service, making them the key target for understanding preferences, satisfaction, and barriers.

contextDemographics.income: Middle to upper-middle income, with disposable income for delivery fees
contextDemographics.household: Urban and suburban households, including families and busy professionals
contextDemographics.geography: Global, with focus on metropolitan areas where delivery is available

assumptions: The category includes both dedicated grocery delivery apps (e.g., Instacart) and retailer-owned delivery services (e.g., Amazon Fresh, Walmart+).
The consumer motion is larger than the B2B motion, but B2B exists (e.g., office snacks, restaurant supplies).
Geographic variation in service availability is handled downstream.

segmentModel.tie_break: bb2 (typical monthly order frequency) is the most direct behavioural self-report that separates regulars (convenience, value, quality) from occasional users, and combined with bb4 (membership) and pe3 (markup tolerance) it resolves ties between convenience and value or quality.
notes: Weights are assigned only to options that clearly discriminate; many options are left unscored.
Each segment has at least two scoring options and at least one 3-point option.
Some options intentionally point to two segments when the behaviour is shared (e.g., high frequency for convenience and value).
3 scoring weight(s) removed: they scored questions that were dropped as duplicates before publication.
segmentModel.excluded: Screening and Profiling questions are excluded from scoring: screeners carry no signal (everyone passed) and demographics are for cross-tabs, not segmentation.

fieldingNotes.recommendedSample: n=800-1,200 for stable segment-level sub-groups (roughly n>=312 per segment after weighting). At n=1,000 the margin of error on a whole-sample percentage is about ±3.1pp at 95% confidence; on a segment of n=200 it widens to about ±6.9pp, so segment-level differences under ~10pp should not be reported as real.
fieldingNotes.quotaControls: Apply quotas on the category-usage and frequency screeners so heavy users — who are more willing survey-takers — are not over-sampled.
scriptingNotes: Rotate the order of answer options on every non-ordinal question to remove primacy bias. Do NOT rotate ordinal scales (frequency bands, price bands, satisfaction) — their order carries meaning.
Anchor 'Other', 'None of these' and 'Prefer not to say' to the bottom of the list, exempt from rotation.
Every 'Other' option takes an open-text capture, coded back into the frame at analysis if any single verbatim exceeds 3%.
No routing or skip logic: every respondent sees every question, so the base is constant across the instrument.
Include one attention check in the middle third — a standard instructed-response item. Terminate on failure and replace.
Randomise the order of the two ranking/trade-off items between respondents so neither is systematically answered while fresher.
caveats: Percentages in this document are simulated from a persona-weighted panel, not fielded with real respondents. Replace with primary data after fielding.
Ranking items are shown as a lighter-weight ranking exercise; run them as MaxDiff if you need more precision on driver importance.
Profiling questions are for cross-tabs only and are excluded from the segmentation scoring model.

metadata.storyline_summary: This survey covers the consumer motion of online grocery delivery in North America. It starts by establishing who the respondent is in terms of their ordering behaviour and household role, then moves through their purchase journey, including triggers, service choice, and spend. It then explores their service requirements and trade-offs, and finally measures satisfaction, pain points, and future intent. The story is designed to separate the four segments based on their frequency, price sensitivity, and quality focus.
storyline_notes: The canonical arc was adapted to focus on service attributes rather than product attributes, since the category is a service.
Added a beat on membership subscription, which is a key differentiator in this market.
Added a beat on fee and markup tolerance, which is a top pain point and a key segment separator.
The 'discovery' beat was reframed as 'service choice and comparison' to reflect how consumers choose between delivery apps.
The 'channel' beat was reframed as 'membership subscription' because the channel is always online; the real choice is which service and whether to subscribe.
The 'quality cues' beat focuses on fresh item quality, a critical concern for online grocery.
metadata.classification_reason: Household consumers buy groceries online, pay for them (either per order or via subscription), and decide what to order. Businesses also purchase through the same platforms for office or commercial use, making it a dual-motion market. The consumer side is the primary and dominant buyer.
